chk_problem.label: accurate
chk_problem.poster_evidence: A benchmark score compares a system output against a reference, yet methodological attention falls almost entirely on the system. The reference is not a constant: it is produced by an annotation process in which people label items, disagree, and have those disagreements resolved by an aggregation rule. A different rule applied to the same human labour can yield a different reference. We invert the usual evaluation design: instead of varying the system and fixing the reference, we hold the scored output fixed and exchange the reference. Any resulting score movement is attributable to reference choice alone.
chk_problem.reason: The poster clearly states the research problem of measuring how reference choice affects scores and model rankings in multilingual benchmarks, aligning with the reference.

chk_conclusion.label: accurate
chk_conclusion.poster_evidence: A benchmark score measures both a system and a reference. Reference sensitivity should therefore be reported alongside the score. Computing it requires no new annotation—only retaining the annotation record and scoring fixed outputs against more than one defensible reference.
chk_conclusion.reason: The poster accurately conveys the paper's conclusion that benchmarks should report a reference-sensitivity band alongside scores to reflect evaluation uncertainty.

chk_limitation.label: accurate
chk_limitation.poster_evidence: All measurements come from one benchmark and one annotation pipeline, so the method transfers but the numerical band does not. The reviewer sample was documented as random, but randomness could not be verified from the export. The export contains no annotator identifiers, preventing separation of differences in skill from differences in convention. The audited subset supports pooled conclusions but gives limited per-language power, while the 135-prompt decontaminated subset is too small for firm conclusions. The scored outputs are human annotation passes, not independently developed model systems, so the magnitude and pattern of reference sensitivity for model predictions remain empirical questions.
